blocks.text: Τηρεὺς γὰρ εἶ σύ; πότερον ὄρνις, ἢ ταώς; [Tēreus gar ei sy? poteron ornis, ē taōs?]

The Epops, namely, had said that he had been Tereus, because Tereus is fabled to have been changed into an ἔποπα [epopa], or upupa [hoopoe]. The Scholiast therefore conjectures that by the name of Tereus Euelpides meant Argus, who was called Τηρεὺς [Tēreus] παρὰ τὸ τηρεῖν τὴν Ἰὼ [para to tērein tēn Iō], and so asked whether he was a peacock, according to the fable which says that Argus was changed into a peacock. But this conjecture is colder than a Gallic winter. Here an allusion to the fable of Argus is sought in vain: Euelpides merely doubts whether the Epops was presenting himself as a hoopoe or as a peacock, because the mark he had assumed in order to be taken for a hoopoe, that is, a crest of feathers, also suits the peacock. Peacocks, however, once so rare in Greece, at length began to be cheap. This is shown by these lines of Antiphanes, a most celebrated poet of Middle Comedy:

Τῶν ταῶν μὲν ὡς ἅπαξ τις ζεῦγος ἤγαγεν μόνον, Σπάνιον ὂν τὸ χρῆμα· πλείους δ᾽ εἰσὶ νῦν τῶν ὀρτύγων. [Tōn taōn men hōs hapax tis zeugos ēgagen monon, spanion on to chrēma; pleious d' eisi nyn tōn ortygōn.]

Once someone brought in just a single pair of peacocks, then a rare bird; but now they are more numerous than quails. The very same happened at Rome, where Hortensius ^{c)} was the first to kill a peacock for food at Rome, at the inaugural banquet of his priesthood. M. Aufidius Lurco was the first to introduce their fattening, around the time of the last war against the pirates, and from [II, 845] that trade he drew an income of sixty thousand sesterces. Against this luxury of the gluttons of his age Publius Syrus inveighs thus in Petronius:
In the gaping maw of luxury the walls of Mars grow slack ^{d)}: For your palate the peacock is kept penned and fed, Clad in its golden Babylonian plumage.

For many, following Hortensius, as Varro testifies in book 3, chapter 6 of his Rustica, raised the prices of peacocks: So that, he says, their eggs sell for five denarii each, and the birds themselves easily for fifty. At these words of Varro Macrobius (Saturnal. book 3, ch. 13) exclaims thus: Behold a thing not only to be wondered at, but to be ashamed of: that peacocks' eggs should sell for five denarii, which today, I will not say sell more cheaply, but do not sell at all! From this it is gathered that the peacock was a foreign bird both at Rome and in Greece. The true homeland of peacocks is of course in India, as we have proved. From there I should think they were first carried over into Persia, Media, and Babylonia; and hence they are called Median and Persian, and are attributed to Babylonia, as we have shown in its place ^{e)}. They were also brought into Judaea under the reign of Solomon, and into Greece not long before Alexander. From there they gradually spread to Rome and the other parts of the West. Since, then, in Job's time India was inaccessible, it is hardly likely that the peacock was known to him or to the Arabs of his age. If anyone replies that it is God who speaks there, to whom all things are known, he will achieve nothing. For God did not prove his power [col. 244] or providence to Job from things unknown to him. 2. Moreover, if the peacock were treated here, a bird so exceptional and something of a marvel, so great a subject would not be dispatched in so few words and so cursorily; nor, in a chapter in which lions, ibexes, wild asses, horses, ostriches, eagles, etc. are each described in many verses, would it be said of the peacock alone, The peacock exults with its wings. And reason scarcely allows the descriptions of the peacock and the ostrich to be joined in the same verse. 3. Why would peacocks be called רננים renanim from their song, when they have an utterly harsh and uncouth voice, which is therefore called a screech by Palladius? ^{f)} So in Phaedrus book 3, fable 57, the peacock complains to Juno that he is laughed at as soon as he utters his voice. 4. The only argument brought forward to prove that the רננים renanim are peacocks, namely that they are said to exult with their wings, proves exactly the contrary, and can be turned forcibly back against those who hold this view. For it is not characteristic of peacocks to exult with their wings, but with their tail. For there lie the jewels by whose splendour it displays itself. Lucretius, book 2:
And the peacock's tail, when it is filled with abundant light, Changes its colours in like manner as it is turned. [II, 846] Ovid, book 15 of the Metamorphoses, fable 35:
Juno's bird, which bears stars on its tail.
Whom the Junonian bird with its jewelled tail could not surpass in appearance. —
The Epigrams of the ancients, where on Gentia and Choë:
When the Junonian bird shakes and spreads its tail, It gracefully bears a thousand eyes, a thousand jewels.
